newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Analysts see Philippine growth as sustainable.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Philippine growth as sustainable.

text.p: Economic growth figures in the Philippines in 1996 show that the country is well on its way to sustained, steady expansion, analysts said on Wednesday.
Concern, however, remains over developments on the political front as a result of the impending 1998 presidential elections, which may hold back some reforms in the economy, they said.
The Philippines earlier reported that gross national product (GNP) registered a growth rate of 6.8 percent in 1996 comapred with 5.0 percent in 1995.
But gross domestic product growth was at 5.5 percent from 4.8 percent in 1995, which was short of a forecast range of 6.0 to 6.8 percent for the year.
"I'mt not surprised. These are sustainable growth rates. It's not discouraging," said Emma Pante, an economist with the Far East Bank and Trust Co.
Far East Bank had expected GNP growth in 1996 at 7.2 percent and GDP at 5.5 percent.
"Our expectations (for 1997) of 6.0 percent GDP and 7.0 to 7.5 percent GNP will be attainable," Pante said.
Jose Mario Cuyegkeng, economist of ING Barings Securities, said the 1996 figures were in line with his expectations for 1996 of 6.9 percent in GNP and 5.5 percent in GDP.
"I think the fourth quarter (slowdown) was expected. The second and third quarters were growing at a blistering pace," he said.
"The economy is still strong and will move up to around 6.0 percent (GDP) in 1997, he said, adding that his GNP forecast is 7.0 percent for this year.
This year, all eyes will be on the political front as potential candidates begin early early campaigning, analysts said.
Socio-economic Planning Secretary Cielito Habito warned that political preoccupation could affect the country's economic agenda.
"There has always been parallelism between political stability and economic growth in the Philippines," Pante said.
"It will affect affect investment interest. It's going to be a concern," Cuyegkeng said.

Nevertheless, "the reforms initiated since 1991 and pursued aggressively by the current administration is difficult to reverse," he said, pointing out that a growing middle-income group had benefitted from such reforms.
Since 1991, the government implemented foreign exchange liberalisation, capital market reforms, and opened up the telecommunications and banking industries.

Far East Bank's Pante said the bigger concern was the country's low domestic savings rate of around 15 percent of GDP versus its East Asian neighbours 30 percent. The savings need to be raised in order to support the heavy infrastructure requirements of the country estimated at $50 billion up to the year 2004, she said.
